CausalChain: Dietary & Environmental Factors + AI-guided Personalized Intervention + Intermittent Nanodelivery of Receptor Modulators -> Modulation of Gut Microbiota Composition (using targeted probiotic and dietary inputs with multi-omics feedback) -> Increased UDCA and Reduced DCA/LCA -> Selective Activation of Nuclear Receptors (FXR, VDR) over Pro-inflammatory Receptors (TGR5) -> Downregulation of NF-κB and MAPK Signaling -> Reduced Epithelial–Mesenchymal Transition and Tumor Proliferation
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that an integrated precision strategy—combining AI-guided personalized dietary and probiotic regimens with intermittent nanodelivery of targeted bile acid receptor modulators and informed by high-resolution metagenomic and metabolomic profiling—can robustly modulate the gut microbiota to shift the bile acid pool toward a tumor-suppressive profile by increasing UDCA relative to DCA and LCA. This tailored bile acid alteration is expected to selectively stimulate FXR and VDR while minimizing TGR5 activation, thereby downregulating NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways. Consequently, this cascade will reduce epithelial–mesenchymal transition and tumor proliferation. The incorporation of dynamic AI algorithms and pilot preclinical studies ensures adaptive intervention management that accounts for individual variability and confounding factors, thereby enhancing both mechanistic insights and translational applicability in cancers such as colorectal and esophageal adenocarcinoma.
Abstract: This study proposes a multi-modal precision intervention that integrates AI-driven personalized dietary and probiotic regimens with strategic nanodelivery of bile acid receptor modulators. Leveraging high-resolution multi-omics (metagenomic and metabolomic) feedback and dynamic AI algorithms, the intervention is designed to modulate the gut microbiota and shift the bile acid pool toward an anticancer profile by increasing ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) while reducing deoxycholic acid (DCA) and lithocholic acid (LCA). The altered bile acid composition is hypothesized to selectively activate tumor-suppressive nuclear receptors such as FXR and VDR over pro-inflammatory receptors like TGR5, thereby downregulating NF-κB/MAPK signaling. This cascade is expected to reduce epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and tumor cell proliferation, particularly in cancers such as colorectal and esophageal adenocarcinoma. The approach not only builds upon established microbial and molecular pathways but also enhances clinical feasibility and mechanistic transparency via pilot preclinical studies and algorithmic stratification of patient-specific variables.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis maintains the original causal chain—intervention leading to gut microbiota modulation, bile acid profile alteration, receptor signaling reprogramming, and downstream inhibition of inflammatory and proliferative pathways—but addresses key limitations highlighted in the review. It introduces an additional layer of controlled intervention via intermittent nanodelivery of receptor modulators, which parallels direct modulation methods observed in the literature, thereby enhancing the practical implementability and clinical control of the strategy. Furthermore, it leverages contemporary AI and multi-omics capabilities to dynamically monitor and adjust the intervention, addresses individual variability and confounding factors through pilot studies, and explicitly lays out the mechanistic steps: from dietary and probiotic modifications to the modulation of UDCA, DCA, and LCA levels, with consequent selective receptor activation leading to reduced EMT and tumor proliferation.
